in writing. − i have agreed to this report because the committee considers that luigi de magistris, in giving the interview, has fulfilled his duties as a member of the european parliament and his political activity by expressing his opinion on a matter of public interest to his constituents. the attempt to prevent members from expressing their views on matters of legitimate public interest and concern and to criticise their political opponents by bringing legal proceedings against them is unacceptable in a democratic society and is contrary to article 8 of the protocol, which aims to protect the freedom of expression of members in the performance of their duties for the benefit of parliament as an institution of the european union. in the light of the foregoing and having regard to rule 6 (3) of the rules of procedure, the committee on legal affairs recommends that the european parliament should uphold the immunity of mr luigi de magistris as a member of parliament.
in writing. - i have agreed to this report because bruno gollnisch's request for immunity does not rely on article 8 of the protocol on the privileges and immunities of the eu and is not applicable in the present case. parliament shall apply its consistent principles when deciding whether to grant or waive the member's immunity. the committee responsible did not find sufficient precise and serious grounds to suspect that the action was brought with the aim of damaging the political reputation of the member. secondly, this case is not within the political sphere of bruno gollnisch's activity as an mep. the case concerned only the activities of bruno gollnisch as a member of the rhône-alpes regional council, which were of a regional and local nature and were different from those of a member of the european parliament. third, mr gollnisch explained the press release of his group in the rhône-alpes regional council, which had been the subject of the complaint, by stating that it had been prepared by the group of the national front in that region, including its head of communications. the application of the member's immunity to such a situation is considered inappropriate, as it would imply the application of overly broad rules aimed at avoiding interference with the activities and independence of parliament. it is therefore for the competent judicial authorities, and not parliament, to decide, in a manner consistent with all democratic guarantees, the extent to which the french laws on incitement to racial hatred have been infringed and the possible legal consequences. the committee on legal affairs considered all the arguments and recommends that the ep should not waive the parliamentary immunity of bruno gollnisch.
in writing. − i have agreed to this document because, first, the committee responsible has not found sufficiently precise and serious suspicions that the action was brought with the aim of damaging the political reputation of a member. second, the case does not fall within the sphere of political activity of mr gollnisch as a member of the european parliament. the case concerned only the activities of bruno gollnisch as a member of the rhône-alpes regional council, which were of a regional and local nature and were different from those of a member of the european parliament. third, mr gollnisch provided an explanation of the press release of his group in the rhône-alpes regional council, which was the subject of the complaint. the application of the member's immunity to such a situation is considered inappropriate, as it would imply the application of overly broad rules aimed at avoiding interference with the activities and independence of parliament. it is therefore for the competent judicial authorities, and not parliament, to decide, in a manner consistent with all democratic guarantees, the extent to which the french laws on incitement to racial hatred have been infringed and the possible legal consequences. it should be noted that the ep, by adopting a decision to waive a member's immunity, simply allows the responsible national authority to hold the person accountable (provided that the activities and independence of the authority are not compromised) and that such a decision does not in any way confirm the member's guilt or express an opinion on whether certain actions or attitudes justify an investigation. the committee on legal affairs also considered all the arguments and recommends that the ep waive the parliamentary immunity of bruno gollnisch.
in writing. − i have endorsed this report because the objective of this agreement is to establish cooperation to ensure the integrated protection of the ecosystem and the sustainable development of the prespa park area, including the development of integrated river basin management plans in line with international and european union standards. the prespa lakes basin (prespa park area) is located in the territories of greece, the former yugoslav republic of macedonia (fyrom) and albania. the first of these countries is a member state of the european union, the second has the status of eu candidate country and the third has the status of potential eu candidate country. albania and the octs have concluded a stabilisation and association agreement with the eu. the prespa park area is a natural area of international importance due to its geomorphological, ecological and cultural importance and its importance in terms of biodiversity. it is a vital habitat for the conservation of many rare and/or endemic species of fauna and flora, as well as globally endangered birds, a transition area and a zone where important archaeological and traditional heritage is protected. for these reasons, the three countries signed, with the eu's participation, on 2 february 2010 an agreement on the protection and sustainable development of the prespa park area, which also requires the consent of the european parliament. to this end, the contracting parties have undertaken, individually and in cooperation, to take the necessary measures and to apply the best available techniques, in accordance with the principles of sovereign equality, territorial integrity, mutual benefit and goodwill.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because it gives parliament its support for the conclusion of the food and agriculture organisation of the united nations agreement to promote the responsible exploitation of fisheries resources and marine ecosystems. this agreement provides for specific measures to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing in eu territorial waters more effectively. these measures are the standards on which member states should base their measures for the monitoring, control and inspection of ships flying a foreign flag and wishing to use their ports. the measures of this agreement could be applied not only to fishing vessels but also to vessels involved in fishing (e.g. transport vessels transporting fishery products). the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing is an essential part of the common fisheries policy and the eu should be able to promote international cooperation in this area by taking an active and constructive part in the adoption of an international instrument on port state measures.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this document as the objective of this agreement is to prevent, deter and eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated (iuu) fishing through the implementation of effective port state measures, thereby ensuring the long-term conservation and sustainable exploitation of living marine resources and marine ecosystems. contracting parties that are port states shall apply this agreement to ships not flying their flags and seeking to call at or in one of their ports. it covers not only fishing vessels but also vessels intended for fishing-related activities, such as transport vessels which may be used for the transport of fishery products. it also establishes a broad definition of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing to cover the widest possible range of unregulated fishing activities. the annexes, which form an integral part of the agreement, specify the information to be provided in advance by a vessel wishing to call at a port of a contracting party, as well as the procedures for inspection, the handling of inspection results, information systems and training requirements. the contracting parties should cooperate to develop, through other relevant multilateral and intergovernmental initiatives, a system for the exchange of information which could be coordinated by the food and agriculture organization (fao) and to facilitate the exchange of information with existing databases relating to this agreement.
in writing. − colleagues, although lithuania is not a large country, the fisheries sector plays an important economic and social role for the small communities in my country. illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing poses a serious threat to the sustainability of lithuanian fisheries. it depletes fish stocks, destroys the marine environment and puts honest fishermen at a disadvantage. in the baltic sea alone, 3800 jobs are threatened each year by illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. according to the pew environment group, lithuanian fishermen are losing more than eur 1.1 million a year to undeclared fishing. this is a very large amount of money considering the size of my country and the fact that these problems are avoidable. unregulated fishing is particularly damaging to the cod fisheries in the baltic sea, which are already in a bad state. cod is the most valuable fish in the baltic sea and most lithuanian fishermen depend on cod resources. unfortunately, our cod fishermen face a 40% rate of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. if illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing were to cease, cod fishing in the baltic sea could recover. however, this requires closing loopholes that allow illegal actors to profit from their activities. we must take stricter sanctions against lawbreakers.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this document because the eu has drawn up legislation which allows actions to be brought in other member states and countries to recognise mutually national court decisions, including the brussels i regulation, the european enforcement order, the small claims procedure, the european order for payment procedure. however, the adoption of a decision is only one part of the process; citizens and businesses must be given the right to seek effective enforcement of their judicial decisions. one of the prerequisites for effective implementation is that the courts must be able to act expeditiously as a temporary measure and order the debtor's assets to be disclosed and frozen. in the absence of such a measure, dishonest traders and other debtors may avoid their obligations by simply transferring their assets to the jurisdiction of another country, thus making it impossible for creditors to enforce court decisions effectively in the common market. the eu institutions have highlighted the need for an effective procedure for the freezing and disclosure of debtors' assets.

in writing. − prior to the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, the member states of the union were mainly governed by bilateral agreements, in particular on investment with third countries. since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, foreign direct investment has become an exclusive competence of the eu and an integrated part of the eu's external trade policy. i agree with this report, which provides for a transitional period to transfer this competence to the eu level, which will in future ensure a high level of investor protection against arbitrary actions by third parties.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because, with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, the eu's common foreign trade policy has become one of the areas of the eu's overall policy in which the eu has exclusive competence. in this way, investment policy, as an area of the common foreign trade policy, must also be coordinated at eu level. currently, member states have bilateral investment agreements with third countries that are partly convergent but often contradictory, which hampers the objectives of the eu's common foreign trade policy and the image of the eu as a single trading area in international and global trade. the main objective of this report is to ensure a smooth transition from an investment policy pursued by individual member states to a common eu investment policy, while ensuring legal certainty for all parties and participants in existing agreements during the transitional period when the old legal regime is replaced by the new regulation. this communication deals in essence with two main issues: the transitional timetable and the cases and procedure for the withdrawal of the authorisation granted by the commission to a member state to negotiate with third parties during the transitional period.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this document as the regulation proposes to establish a power for the commission to withdraw authorisation and to require member states to renegotiate or terminate dis (bilateral investment treaties) and to obtain the commission's consent before negotiating new dis. it also sets out the conditions as to how, when and what can be negotiated. with the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, foreign direct investment was included in the list of areas falling under the common commercial policy. pursuant to article 3 (1) (e) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, the union has exclusive competence in the field of the common commercial policy. only the union can therefore adopt legally binding acts in this area. member states themselves may do so only if they are empowered by the union in accordance with article 2 (1) of the treaty. the union's exercise of its competence in developing a common investment policy, the main objective of which is to provide the best possible investment protection for all investors in the member states and to ensure a level playing field for investment in third country markets, will further develop this relationship. as the new investment policy will be developed taking into account the existence of bilateral investment agreements between member states during the transitional period, it should recognise the rights of investors covered by those agreements and ensure legal certainty. the commission should take the necessary steps to ensure that all existing bilateral investment agreements between member states are gradually replaced by new eu-wide agreements.

one of the causes of the chernobyl disaster was a design error and a failed test of the reactor under extreme conditions. a quarter of a century later, the tragedy in japan forced us to test the safety of existing nuclear facilities. i have no doubt that the european union's power plants will pass these tests, or at least pass them. however, in the case of accidents at such facilities, the damage to the environment and to people does not stop at national borders. the whole of europe learned that lesson well 25 years ago. therefore, the tests must also be carried out at nuclear power plants outside the european union. two power plants are currently being planned in the vicinity of the european union's borders, one in belarus and the other in the kaliningrad region. unfortunately, it seems premature to talk about any kind of resistance testing for them. in their case, even the environmental impact assessment was not properly carried out, all concerns were not addressed, and a system of compensation for environmental damage was not established. moreover, the construction of the belarusian power plant is planned in the area where the largest earthquake in the history of belarus with a magnitude of 7 occurred. the european union as a whole, both the commission and the member states, must therefore act in solidarity to ensure that power plants planned in the european union's neighbourhood are subject to the same resistance tests as those applied to power plants in the european union. also that, through the mediation of international organisations, atena, the espo convention secretariat, the project promoters provide clear and reasoned answers without delay on the choice of sites, environmental impact, compensation and evacuation plans. only then can we be sure that we do not have to evacuate 100,000 people, this time within the european union.
this is a very important debate, but i think it's too late. the nuclear disaster at chernobyl continues to have devastating consequences not only for the people of ukraine but also for those of neighbouring countries. the people of lithuania are still paying for this disaster with their health; its effects will also be felt by future generations. sadly, the fukushima disaster showed that in those 25 years, the world had failed to make an objective assessment of the nuclear threat for the sake of material gain. we have been told for years that nuclear energy is the cleanest and safest, but in the event of a disaster, we see that the consequences are devastating, that they will be felt for generations, and that the cost of such consequences is incalculable. the nuclear safety issue needs to be fundamentally reviewed. the commission's initiative to introduce load testing in nuclear power plants in the european union is welcome, but such control must become systematic and permanent rather than episodic in order to minimise the likelihood of accidents. the lessons of the banking crisis show that no single institution or sector can effectively self-regulate and self-monitor itself. i think you will agree, commissioner, that it is therefore essential that a nuclear security policy be drawn up and monitored as soon as possible at european union level. we must have our own european union position vis-à-vis third countries which intend to build nuclear power stations right on the european union's external borders. we need to know what action will be taken if the nuclear power plants fail to meet the requirements of the load tests, and many other questions.
member of the commission. − in reply to the first question, access in areas of libya where military operations are taking place is limited but we still – thanks to the courage of humanitarian workers – have been able to reach two affected populations in misrata as well as in the contested cities in the coastal area. where we have not been able to reach affected populations is in the western part of libya under the control of gaddafi. we are also very concerned that we are now seeing an increase of libyans fleeing the country. out of the 740 000 people i mentioned today, some 50 000 are libyans and it is their number that is growing, facing us with an additional challenge to help these people. most of them are moving to live with host communities in tunisia and in egypt. we now have to find a way to support these communities. as far as the ceasefire is concerned, we have been calling for a ceasefire to allow safe access for humanitarian assistance and, of course, we very much support the un in this regard. i can assure you that we are in constant contact with the un and the unhcr so that we can deploy assistance when a window of opportunity opens up, as we have now done on numerous occasions, for example in the case of misrata. there was actually a separate question on the coordinated response. may i continue with an answer to this question? we have made significant progress in advancing work on the communication on strengthening the eu disaster response that was unanimously supported by the council at the end of last year. our intention is to actually accelerate work on implementing this communication with an eye to setting up a 24/7 european emergency response centre by the end of this calendar year. it will be built on the basis of the current mic – the monitoring and information centre – and also on the basis of the emergency teams of humanitarian assistance that existed in echo. it will have the physical capability to operate on a 24/7 basis. over the last year, especially in the context of the response to the haiti disaster, the pakistan floods and today in response to libya, we have built very strong and effective working relations with the eu military staff in the european external action service to the point that now eu military staff designate liaison officers as part of our humanitarian operation, so we can make sure that we plan and execute together as one. to give a straightforward answer to your question: yes, we are making progress. unfortunately, due to the events of the last year, we have faced exceptionally difficult circumstances in 2010 – and also this year – that have given a very strong impetus to advance this work.
member of the commission. − the european union is one of the major donors of food assistance. the commission has been committed to providing leadership in ensuring that the most vulnerable people in crisis have access to safe, adequate and nutritious food. the commission does not implement aid operations itself. it provides funding to partner organisations – the un agencies, international ngos, the red cross family – or partners who have vast experience in carrying out aid operations among the most vulnerable people. our implementing partners have the authority to decide what the most appropriate food assistance needs are in any specific circumstance. we encourage them to purchase food locally as much as possible. why? because, by doing so, they provide useful assistance to local farmers and we do not end up feeding the people yet, at the same time, killing the livelihoods of the local farmers by providing our own food. the commission is always validating these choices and making sure that factors, such as the availability and nutritious quality of commodities, dietary habits of the local populations, availability of cooking facilities and cost considerations, including transportation costs, are taken into account. on that basis the exact composition of our food assistance will be determined. obviously canned food has its advantages, including canned fish, because it can hold for a prolonged period of time and is therefore suitable for managing stocks. it also has some disadvantages, which are sometimes related to costs or dietary habits in local populations. so we always have to be sure that what we are doing is helping people in the most effective way.
member of the commission. − the point you are making is very valid. we need to look at high nutritional value and also simplicity of use. at the same time, what i would like to caution against is expanding the intervention of the commission in deciding up front what exactly should be the composition of food assistance in any given circumstance. we have taken a very important leadership role in the european union with regard to food assistance by untying our food assistance or, in other words, not making it a requirement that european food assistance includes food produced in europe. sometimes agricultural surpluses from europe are used in food assistance. we do require that food provided to people in any circumstance is the most appropriate for the particular circumstances. and why do we do that? when we untie our food aid, this allows our partner organisations to purchase food locally and provides an incentive for local farmers. we do not end up bringing food from europe, killing the livelihoods of local farmers and then giving them development assistance and actually bringing even more food because we have been unwise in our approach to food assistance. i can assure you that, globally, what europe has done in this respect is seen as the right thing to do and we are applauded by people in developing countries and by our development partners for taking this approach to food assistance. having said that, we also support prepositioning of food, in which case canned fish is very appropriate. i can assure you that we strive to do the right thing. when it is the right thing we of course encourage it to be done. you are very welcome to visit our services – we are always very happy to interact with the european parliament.
member of the commission. − what the council conclusions gave us a mandate to do is to work towards the establishment of european civil protection capacity that is predictable and ready for immediate deployment, based on our member states dedicating modules that we can mobilise and transport to where they are needed immediately, as the disaster hits. where we are today is actually quite impressive because we already have 104 modules that member states have registered with us and we have their commitment that we can mobilise and deliver assistance in a predictable manner, as long as they do not need these modules to fight the same disasters at home. we still have work to do in identifying the gaps and how we are going to fill these gaps. for that we will do the prudent work and then come to our authorising environment, to the council and to parliament, for your approval of the approach we are proposing to fill gaps. what is advancing faster than anticipated last year is the creation of the european emergency response centre. i can assure you it would make a big difference because it would allow us to accelerate work on scenario planning – what kinds of disasters we have to be prepared for, and also on modelisation of the committed member states’ assets. the words that made a difference were ‘voluntary commitment from member states’. but once that commitment is made, these assets belong to the community and they are deployable by us.
member of the commission. − both agriculture and forestry can, of course, play an important role in achieving the eu’s climate objectives, and non-co2 greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture are actually included in the eu’s effort sharing mechanism, but emissions and removals of co2 related to land use, land-use change and forestry (what we call lulucf) are not part of the current reduction commitment as adopted back in the 2008 in the climate and energy package. however, as part of the package, the commission was requested by the european council and parliament to assess modalities for their inclusion in the eu reduction commitment by mid-2011, and to make a legislative proposal as appropriate. so the commission plans to publish the relevant communication this summer, i.e. in a very short time from now. inclusion could strengthen the environmental integrity of our climate commitments, ensuring that all emissions and removals are covered, while enhancing the visibility of efforts by farmers and foresters to increase sinks through sustainable land-use management. the current cap includes instruments that address climate change, mainly through the multiple co-benefits between agri-environmental policies and climate action. pillar one provides income support to farmers who have to respect cross-compliance – a concept that includes baseline obligations, some of which are relevant to climate action. rural development policy in pillar two makes more targeted climate-change measures available to member states. the 2008 health check reconfirmed climate change as one of the major challenges to be addressed, and already measures in relation to forestry – for example, afforestation – can be supported under the rural development policy. a reformed cap with a greener first pillar, introducing non-contractual and annual environmental actions that go beyond cross-compliance, and a second pillar more focused on climate action, supported by a professional farm advisory service, could be tailored towards helping farmers to manage their land-use systems so as to contribute to climate action (mitigation), and also become less vulnerable to climate change (adaptation). that is definitely what we intend to achieve through the next cap.
member of the commission. − basically i think that we agree. you use the word ‘compensation’. i prefer to say that we should have the common agricultural policy move more towards a situation where there would be some help available for people who are delivering something to the common good. it thus becomes a much more tangible and more concrete option for farmers to move in the direction of doing something for the climate, for water quality, or whatever, so that we get more value for the subsidies that we give to agriculture. that is, at least, the thrust of our thinking in the commission.

in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because it is necessary to amend the rules of procedure of the european parliament by creating a joint parliament-commission transparency register. i would like to emphasise that, since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, the european parliament's powers have been strengthened, since it has become one of the legislators in almost all areas under the ordinary legislative procedure. these new developments have thus attracted even more attention from representatives of interest groups, who play a key role in the implementation of an open and pluralistic dialogue and are an important source of information for members of parliament in relation to the exercise of their mandate. in view of these developments and in line with their transparency commitments, the european parliament and the european commission have agreed to establish and maintain a common register to register and monitor organisations and individuals involved in the formulation and implementation of european union policies. this register is intended to ensure that meps are able to exercise their parliamentary powers without restriction and that their constituents are not prevented from entering the european parliament's premises.
in writing. − i have supported this document because the relationship between the european institutions and policy-makers on the one hand and civil society, citizens and representative associations on the other is regulated and promoted by the eu treaty, in particular by article 11 (1) and (2) thereof: 1.the institutions shall, by appropriate means, give citizens and representative associations the opportunity to express and exchange their views on all areas of union activity. 2.the institutions shall maintain an open, transparent and permanent dialogue with representative associations and civil society. since the ratification of the treaty of lisbon, parliament's powers have been strengthened and it has become one of the legislators in almost all areas under the ordinary legislative procedure, thus attracting an even greater number of representatives of interest groups, which, moreover, play a key role in the implementation of the open and pluralistic dialogue on which the democratic system is based and are an important source of information for members of parliament in relation to the exercise of their mandate. in the light of these developments and in this constitutional context, the ep and the commission agreed to set up and maintain a common register to register and monitor organisations and individuals involved in the formulation and implementation of eu policies. it should be noted that the register must ensure that members are entitled to exercise their parliamentary powers without restriction and that their constituents are not prevented from entering parliament's premises. furthermore, it may not infringe the powers or prerogatives of the parties and affect their powers to organise their activities.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report. this is a first step towards greater transparency in the work of the institutions and in ensuring the provisions of the union's public administration. the transparency register, as it will henceforth be called, remains optional, but individuals or organisations engaged in lobbying activities will be required to register if they wish to gain access to the european parliament. registered entities will also have to declare their financial sources and their interests and legislative proposals. this will increase transparency and provide more detailed information on individuals or organisations who approach members of the european parliament with certain questions or proposals. i believe that negotiations with the council should continue so that it can join the transparency register and become a common register for all three institutions.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because transparency of political institutions is a necessary condition for their legitimacy. it is necessary to examine how decisions are made, which forces influence them and, finally, how the finances, i.e. taxpayers' money, are distributed. the rules governing lobbying are therefore a matter of legality. the european parliament is the first institution of the european union to have taken note of the growing number of interest groups operating at european level, and it is therefore necessary to examine all the possible consequences of this phenomenon. following the european parliament elections, a new working group of the european parliament and the commission was set up, which already approved the draft agreement on the establishment of the transparency register in november 2010. the new draft makes the register optional, but at present only registered representatives of interest groups are allowed on the premises of the european parliament. the single transparency register ensures the participation of a wide range of actors and provides more opportunities for non-commercial organisations to carry out their activities. i believe that this common register is another step towards greater transparency in the european union's institutions and, at the same time, greater trust in the work of the institutions by citizens.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this document because the transparency of political institutions is a necessary condition for their legitimacy. it must be easy to scrutinise how decisions are made, which forces influence them and, finally, how resources, i.e. taxpayers' money, are allocated. the rules governing lobbying are therefore a matter of legality. the results achieved are in line with parliament's objectives as set out in the main points: firstly, although the register is optional (parliament sought to make it compulsory), it can be considered de facto compulsory, as only registered representatives of interest groups are allowed access to parliament's premises on a permanent basis; secondly, the common register ensures the participation of a wide range of categories of entities and respects their distinct and specific identity. the new transparency register provides more opportunities for non-profit organisations to be included in it; thirdly, the new system contains additional information such as the number of persons involved in all activities related to the register and the eu funds received in the course of registration. the activities that may be covered by the register and the complaints procedure will also be clarified. i think it was necessary to approve the draft agreement on the establishment of a transparency register. the single register will be another step towards greater transparency in the european institutions and is likely to contribute to greater trust of european citizens in the european project.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report. the proper functioning of the internal market depends on the stability of the financial system and the confidence of european citizens and consumers in financial institutions and transactions. the recent financial crisis has led to the collapse of many financial institutions worldwide, at great cost to taxpayers. i support the commission's initiative to critically examine the stability of financial institutions and the financial system as a whole and their regulatory and supervisory framework, so that a similar situation does not recur in the future and the financial sector meets the needs of the real economy and demonstrates the highest possible level of social responsibility.
in writing. − i voted for this report because it is the european parliament's contribution to the debate on how to ensure more effective governance of financial institutions in europe. this debate is crucial in seeking ways to avoid a repeat of the global financial and economic crisis of 2008 and beyond. the failure of the sfcs has been and continues to be costly for taxpayers and it is therefore necessary to examine the causes of the problems that have arisen. in its report, the european parliament, in response to the commission's green paper on improving the governance of financial institutions, gives considerable attention to the need to regulate more strictly the appointment of persons in charge, the setting of criteria for the competence and aptitude test of members of the board of directors and the means of ensuring their independence. the communication also proposes to establish mandatory risk oversight committees at the level of company boards and calls for a requirement for financial institutions to disclose recovery plans and supervisory reports of the institution, as well as to prepare reports on the adequacy and effectiveness of internal control systems and to include similar reports in the annual report prepared by the external auditor.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this document because the financial sector should respond to the needs of the real economy, help to promote sustainable growth and demonstrate the highest degree of social responsibility. it is important to note that the behaviour of certain financial market participants and institutions is characterised by a lack of values and ethics. financial markets and institutions should take into account the interests of all stakeholders, such as their customers, shareholders and employees, when implementing their corporate social responsibility policies. effective risk management is one of the key factors in preventing future crises. the commission considers that the measure is imputable to the state and that the measure is imputable to the state. i think it is necessary to set up compulsory risk monitoring committees or to provide for a corresponding structure. the risk should not be disproportionate.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this important resolution on the state of play of the negotiations on the eu-india free trade agreement. india is an important trading partner of the eu: in 2000, india was the 17th most important trading partner of the european union, and in 2010 it was the 8th. in addition, india is the largest beneficiary of the generalised scheme of preferences (gsp) and european union imports from india under preferential tariffs or zero duties were worth eur 19,9 billion in 2009 and accounted for 83% of all eu imports from india. both sides hope to benefit greatly from the abolition of tariffs, trade in services and the liberalisation of business creation, but i have to agree with the disappointment expressed in the resolution at the slow pace of negotiations on a free trade agreement (fta). both parties should make every effort to conclude a comprehensive, ambitious and harmonised epa by 2011, as this agreement would provide opportunities to increase eu-india trade and investment, to develop business, and to increase eu-india combined exports and imports in line with the epa. i agree with the position expressed in the resolution that if eu-india economic cooperation is based on shared universal values, it can become a model for cooperation with other countries.
in writing. - i voted for this resolution. after more than three years of negotiations, the eu and india have reached a crucial stage in the negotiations on a free trade agreement, with the finalisation of the negotiations on the most important sectors. however, some very important issues need to be resolved in a very clear way in the further negotiations. i believe that the most sensitive sectors in europe, such as industry, agriculture and the service sector, should be given special attention. india is one of the largest economies in the world, with a fast-growing service sector. it has a strong interest in entering the eu services market and therefore it is necessary to carry out a thorough assessment of how a free trade agreement could affect the eu services sector (and other important sectors) and employment. at the same time, it is necessary to ensure that future trade policy is conducted in accordance with the objectives of the european union, including binding commitments on social and environmental standards, at all stages of the negotiations.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the document because the eu is india's largest source of foreign direct investment. both parties expect to benefit substantially from the abolition of tariffs, trade in services and the liberalisation of business start-ups and reaffirm their commitment to lower tariffs and further liberalisation of business start-ups and trade in services. access to the market is restricted by non-tariff barriers to trade such as health and safety requirements, technical barriers, quantitative restrictions, conformity procedures, trade defence mechanisms, customs procedures, internal taxes, failure to adopt international norms and standards. the eu and india must commit to accelerating the negotiations on the tpp and to making substantial and effective progress towards a swift conclusion of an ambitious and coherent multilateral trade and investment agreement. both parties should make every effort to achieve a comprehensive, ambitious and harmonised gpa by 2011. the agreement must take account of the sensitive aspects relating to trade in agricultural products, but should not thereby impede the opening of markets in complementary areas. the commission should take due account of any negative impact on european agriculture, in particular in areas such as market opening, gmos, the dairy sector, the beef sector, the protection of intellectual property and the indication of origin. the commission should also negotiate effective and transparent procurement systems, and india should apply transparent and fair procurement procedures and provide access to procurement systems for european companies.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this important resolution on eu-japan trade relations. the eu and japan are important partners and investors in each other's economies, with a combined volume of foreign direct investment of €200 billion in 2009. japan is the eu's sixth largest trading partner and the eu is japan's third largest trading partner. i agree that the time has come to conclude an eu-japan free trade agreement (fta), but before the negotiations can begin, japan must seriously commit to removing the non-tariff barriers that restrict european companies' access to the market, i.e. barriers to public procurement, insufficient recognition of international standards for medical devices and more favourable conditions for national leaders in financial services. the negative impact of non-tariff barriers means that the eu's bilateral trade with japan is smaller than most of the eu's trade with other major trading partners. i support the resolution's view that the eu and japan's gsps can benefit both countries and their economies.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because i fully agree that the eu can and must contribute to the accelerated recovery of the japanese economy following the recent devastation by the worst natural disaster in the country's history. the communication calls on the commission to develop a specific framework under which the eu, through various aspects of international trade, can continue to contribute to countries affected by natural disasters. in the case of japan in particular, the european parliament resolution proposes to exploit the opportunities offered by international public procurement and service markets, given the increased interest shown by the eu and its member states in these areas. many barriers to public procurement and trade services still arise from legitimate national regulation, and the report proposes to overcome these barriers by working towards a better understanding of the approaches of the mutual regulatory systems. however, the report points out that investment and trade in services must be included in discussions on trade with japan in order to ensure that further market opening does not conflict with either european or japanese rules on public services and environmental and cultural diversity.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the document because in 2009 the eu and japan together generated more than a quarter of global gdp and were responsible for more than 20% of world trade, and japan and the eu are important investors in each other's economies. the council and the commission have noted that japan's ability to remove regulatory barriers to trade is a precondition for the opening of negotiations on an eu-japan free trade agreement (fta) to promote closer economic integration between the two strategic trading partners. a multilateral trading system based on wto principles is the most effective means of achieving open and fair trade worldwide. i believe that the european union and japan should contribute to the successful conclusion of the negotiations on the doha development agenda. the eu-japan fta would not only benefit from increased bilateral trade in goods and services, but also foster cooperation on eu horizontal priorities such as cooperation on innovation, regulatory cooperation and the fight against market abuse, as well as cooperation on a wide range of environmental issues, among others.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this resolution on the commission's green paper on the protection and information of forests in the european union. deforestation and climate change the european parliament has endorsed the provisions set out in this green paper, but it is necessary to strengthen the eu's forest strategy, and this strengthening should be aimed at improving the management and conservation of forests, that this strategy should be directed both towards forest protection and towards the use of sustainable timber resources, as forests offer opportunities to address climate change. it should be noted that, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, the primary responsibility for the forest strategy should remain with the member states, but the european union should be more active in supporting, coordinating and complementing member states' actions in the field of forestry policy, taking into account the different regional conditions. this policy should be implemented in order to ensure the sustainable development of the forestry sector and contribute to improving the standard of living of european citizens and to promoting the development of rural areas.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report. forests and woodland cover 42% of the eu's territory. the forest industry has a turnover of around eur 300 billion and creates over 2 million jobs, mainly in rural areas, thus contributing to economic growth, jobs and prosperity through the provision of timber and the creation of tourism opportunities. eu mice are facing major threats to their survival, including climate change, new pests, increased fire risks (especially in the mediterranean region) and human activities (increasing demand for wood biomass for energy), which are leading to their extinction. i agree that the commission and the member states need to do more to achieve the environmental and quality of life objectives of the eu action plan for the mushroom, which is currently lagging behind. the eu forestry strategy and the eu plan for mouse should also be updated to include the climate change dimension and broader forest protection issues.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because it is the european parliament's response to the commission's green paper on the launch of a public consultation on forest protection and forest preparedness for climate change across the european union. in its communication, parliament welcomes the commission's green paper and calls for an update of the eu forestry strategy, while taking due account of the application of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality and incorporating the climate change aspect and other broader forest protection issues. parliament also reaffirmed its view that more resources should be allocated to forest protection measures under the rural development pillar of the cap, especially in the light of the new challenges posed by climate change. among other possible sources of funding, the report also proposes to consider the possibility of setting up payments to companies for ecosystem functions that contribute to the conservation of biodiversity and the protection of forests. amongst many other measures, such as strengthening coordination at eu level and the exchange of information between member states, the commission is also invited to consider the possibility of legislating a ban on building in areas where it has been proven that forest fires have been deliberately set.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the document because the eu's forests and other wooded land cover more than 42% of the eu's territory. forests are the livelihood of millions of workers, entrepreneurs and 16 million forest owners. the forestry sector provides more than 2 million jobs, mainly to smes. 350,000 people work in forestry. the eu deforestation-to-growth ratio is stable at around 60%. in several member states, this ratio is expected to increase to more than 100%, leading to a decrease in the total volume of wood after 2020. european forests and forestry are managed according to different regional and national models, grouped according to their production and protection orientation. forests serve both as resources and as ecosystems. it is proposed that mandatory programmes be drawn up. the aid must also be targeted, i.e. linked to climate change. the proposals include: long-term competitiveness, environmental improvement and protection, improvement of the quality of life, promotion of coordination and communication. we must do everything we can to conserve and use this resource sustainably, so that our future generations can enjoy it, and to contribute to reducing environmental pollution.

in writing. − i voted in favour of the resolution on the development of the common security and defence policy following the entry into force of the lisbon treaty. it is important to stress that the new csdp introduced by the lisbon treaty provides a firm political statement about the union’s intention to act as a force for stability in the world. i support the position that current economic austerity and the provisions of the lisbon treaty may help member states towards smarter spending on defence by pooling and sharing a larger proportion of their defence capabilities, budget and requirements while achieving more security for their citizens, although the reality is that the economic and financial crisis affects eu national defence budgets, programmes and force structures and therefore, more than one year after the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, there are not yet clear signs of a post-lisbon eu holistic approach enabling traditional procedural and institutional barriers to be overcome. therefore, it is important that member states find appropriate means for the implementation of the csdp as the lisbon treaty provides a framework for upgrading cooperation on defence whilst achieving economies of scale, maintaining strategic relevance and providing security for the union’s citizens.

the small business act of 2008 was intended to give a boost to its development and to improve business conditions in europe. much has been done to improve its environment and simplify administrative requirements, for example with the adoption of the directive on electronic invoicing or the directive on late payment. but that's not enough. today we see that the results are not what small businesses had hoped for. key priorities such as financing, simplification of regulatory frameworks, improvement of the business environment are not being implemented in a systematic and consistent manner. and the business environment varies widely across member states. the different legal regimes for the protection of consumers' rights that have survived to date reduce consumer confidence in the single market and discourage businesses from developing their activities in other member states. this in essence prevents the creation of a more business-friendly and favourable internal market in the european union. the economic and financial crisis has hit small businesses hardest. we see companies that are going bankrupt or are heavily indebted. we had measures in place to help them, but unfortunately they did not always work out. the commission's 'progress' microfinance facility was indeed a very appropriate step to provide access to finance for small businesses in times of crisis. however, as various studies have shown, in some member states, national banks have made the conditions for granting loans even more stringent than they have been in the case of business loans. the european investment bank, which administered these loans for two years, had no data at all on the implementation of this measure. the question is, why do we need such a mediator at all? i wanted to say a few words about the 'jewish youth' initiative. the aim of this initiative is very attractive, as mobility will be used to improve the education and training of young people and to facilitate the transition from education to the labour market. this is particularly relevant today for young people, who are one of the social groups most affected by the global financial crisis. youth must be helped to enter the labour market to secure their future and contribute to economic growth and prosperity. young people must be given opportunities to develop competencies, skills and knowledge that they can use in the future to actively contribute to the growth and sustainable future of our european union. i think it is equally important to ensure that the education received is in line with the needs of the labour market. it is also important that the opportunities for european young people to develop and contribute to the prosperity of the european union are not reduced in the future. there are also some problems with mobility. young people who have completed their education in another member state often remain to live and work there. as a result, a country like lithuania, whose economic situation is not easy, risks losing for a while the educated people who are the basis of the country's growth, not only in economic terms. it is true that this is an internal problem that we will solve ourselves. and it's very good that we're trying to address a problem that's relevant to young people today.
the process of early childhood education is one of the most important responsibilities of both parents and state institutions. in this context, it is important and appropriate that the resolution stresses the importance of early teaching of regional and minority languages. the mother tongue is especially important, since it is the language in which children form their thoughts and acquire knowledge. therefore, it is unacceptable to introduce in the schools of indigenous national minorities, teaching in a non-native language of some subjects from the first or second grade, as recently passed in the lithuanian parliament. the forced introduction of bilingual subjects is clearly perceived by the local poles living in lithuania for seven centuries as discrimination that should be put to an end.

for the alde group the 1941 mass deportations of the baltic population was one of the most dramatic and tragic events of the 20th century. the blow to lithuania, latvia and estonia, to their political communities and to their very civilized life, isolated these peoples and countries for five decades. it also dealt a major blow to european solidarity and european togetherness. this isolation ended only in 1991, when it was possible to speak of a break in the history of the baltic peoples. but it was not until 2004 that the accession of the baltic states to the european union really marked and ended the division of europe. the deliberate targeting of innocent civilians, mostly the most educated, the most advanced people, is an integral part of the social engineering of the stalin era and the struggle against individuals and nations, their memory and dignity. and yet, we can end up optimistically, because today, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we can commemorate seven decades of the slaughter of innocent people in the baltic states, and the fact that we recognise this is restoring europe's dignity, solidarity and our consolidated political memory.

noise pollution and traffic congestion, are becoming more serious. they therefore have an increasing role to play in innovative, professional policy measures such as encouraging the use of environmentally friendly vehicles or developing route planners. measures to internalise external costs are expected to increase economic efficiency and reduce negative environmental impacts. the fair white paper entitled 'roadmap to a single european transport area, towards a competitive and resource-efficient transport system'. the measure is the first step towards the internalisation of the vice-president of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, after three years’ negotiations, we are now close to the adoption of the amended directive on charging heavy goods vehicles, the so-called eurovignette directive. this is part of a wider strategy to internalise the external costs of transport in all modes to get transport prices right. i would like to thank the belgian presidency for unblocking this file in the council. the hungarian presidency skilfully negotiated with a very narrow majority in the council. let me thank in particular the rapporteur, mr el khadraoui. together with the shadow rapporteurs and members of the committee on transport and tourism, he managed to significantly improve the text at second reading. i look forward to parliament adopting this directive for two main reasons. firstly, to achieve our goals of a more sustainable green transport system and thus implement the polluter-pays principle. the directive will authorise member states to charge tolls on lorries not only for infrastructure costs, as is the case now, but also for noise and air pollution. it will also allow more efficient varying of tolls to ease congestion during peak hours. secondly, at a time of scarce public funding, the charging for external costs provided by the new directive will generate revenues and make new financial resources available for transport infrastructure. the commission supports this agreement. i have noted your declaration on the correlation table. i fully sympathise with you on this issue. on behalf of the commission i will also make a formal statement: ‘the commission recalls its commitment towards ensuring that member states establish correlation tables linking the transposition measures they adopt to the eu directive and that they communicate them to the commission in the framework of transposing eu legislation in the interests of citizens, better law-making and increasing legal transparency, and to assist in the examination of the conformity of national rules with eu provisions. ‘ the commission regrets the lack of support for the provision included in the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 1999/62/ec on the charging of heavy goods vehicles for the use of certain infrastructures, which aimed at rendering the establishment of correlation tables obligatory. ‘ the commission, in a spirit of compromise and in order to ensure the immediate adoption of that proposal, can accept the substitution of the obligatory provision on correlation tables included in the text with the relevant recital encouraging member states to follow this practice. it will inform parliament within 12 months of the adoption of this agreement in plenary and produce a report at the end of the transposition period on practice in the member states, in order to draw up for themselves – and in the interests of the union – their own tables illustrating as far as possible the correlation between this directive and the transposition measures and to make them public. however, the position followed by the commission in this file shall not be considered as a precedent. the commission will continue its efforts with a view to finding, together with parliament and the council, an appropriate solution to this horizontal institutional issue.’

in writing. freedom of movement is one of the eu's most important values for all citizens of the european union, and the schengen area is unique in that it abolishes common border controls between its member states and implements the free movement of persons. we must therefore respect the right to free movement of all citizens of the european union without exception. if bulgaria and romania are subject to additional criteria than other eu member states due to their accession to the schengen area, this will create a double standard. we must avoid a system based on 'double standards' that is too strict for candidate countries and too soft for countries that already belong to the schengen area. the schengen rules must be the same for all countries and the evaluation system must be based on the provision that the rules must be respected at all times, not just at the time of accession. the countries acceding to the schengen area must continue to comply with all security requirements, since the security of that area depends on the strict and effective control of the external borders by the member states and on the rapid and high-quality exchange of information through the schengen information system. it is therefore necessary for member states to cooperate to the greatest extent possible and to take the necessary measures to abolish internal border controls, in particular in the context of increasing migratory flows, since the security of the schengen area depends on the rigour and effectiveness of the controls carried out by each member state at its external borders.

liberalise their labour markets when the second phase expires on 31 december 2011. the end of transitional arrangements means that more eu citizens can take advantage of one of the eu’s fundamental freedoms and work freely in another member state. that opens great opportunities for the individual, who can move where there are jobs, and also for the economy. i know that mobility and freedom of movement for workers are also important to this house. the commission is pleased with the own-initiative report on promoting worker mobility within the european union and is following the debate in the parliamentary committees with great interest. but we are also aware that, despite the large body of eu legislation in the area of freedom of movement for workers, most eu citizens still feel there are too many obstacles to working in another member state. the situation has been highlighted on several occasions recently. the monti report of 9 may 2010 – ‘a new strategy for the single market’ – points out that, while freedom of movement for workers is a success overall from a legal viewpoint, it is the least-used of our four single market freedoms. tackling these problems calls for a broad approach, combined with effective implementation of the principle of free movement. the enforceability of the right of free movement conferred by eu law is particularly relevant in cases of discrimination on the basis of nationality, as the individuals concerned need to have suitable mechanisms to ensure such rights are properly protected. the commission services are currently evaluating eu legislation on the free movement of workers, and in particular regulation (eec) no 1612/68, and are exploring the options for improving the enforcement of eu law on freedom of movement, including, where necessary, by presenting an initiative in 2012. parliament’s report on worker mobility therefore comes at the right time, and will certainly contribute to the debate on enforcement of eu law on free movement of workers and the choice of any further action on this issue.
